==English==

===Etymology===
{{bor+|en|sco|bauther}}, {{m|sco|bather|t=to bother}}. Origin {{unk|en|nocap=1}}. Perhaps related to {{cog|sco|pother|t=to make a stir or commotion, bustle}}, also of unknown origin. Compare {{cog|en|pother|t=to poke, prod}}, variant of {{m|en|potter|t=to poke}}. More at {{m|en|potter}}. Perhaps related to {{cog|ga|bodhaire|t=noise}}, {{cog|ga|bodhraim|t=to deafen, annoy}}.<ref>Concise Oxford English Dictionary 2011</ref>

===Pronunciation===

* {{IPA|en|/ˈbɒðɚ/|a=CA}}
* {{IPA|en|a=NY,Italian American,somewhat <<dated>>|[ˈbɑɾə]}}

* {{IPA|en|/ˈbɒðə/|[ˈbɔ̟ðə]|~|[ˈbɞ̠ðə]|a=NZ}}
* {{rhymes|en|ɒðə(ɹ)|ɑːðə(ɹ)|a2=father-bother|s=2}}

===Verb===
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[annoy]], to [[disturb]], to [[irritate]]; to be [[troublesome]] to, to make [[trouble]] for.
#: {{syn|en|annoy|disturb|inconvenience|irritate|put out|vex|Thesaurus:annoy|Thesaurus:upset}}
#: {{ux|en|Would it '''bother''' you if I smoked?}}
## {{lb|en|imperative|euphemistic}} [[damn|Damn]]; [[curse]].
# {{lb|en|intransitive|or|reflexive}} To feel [[care]] or [[concern]]; to [[burden#Verb|burden]] or [[inconvenience#Verb|inconvenience]] oneself out of concern.
#: {{syn|en|care|mind|Thesaurus:care}}
#: {{ux|en|I never '''bother''' about such trivialities.}}
#: {{ux|en|I wouldn't '''bother''' with an umbrella if I were you.}}
#* {{RQ:James American|page=87|passage=To expand, without '''bothering''' about it—without shiftless timidity on one side, or loquacious eagerness on the other—to the full compass of what he would have called a "pleasant" experience, was Newman's most definite programme of life.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive|catenative}} To [[take the trouble]], to [[trouble#Verb|trouble oneself]] (to do something).
#: {{syn|en|go to the trouble|take the trouble}}
#: {{ux|en|Why do I even '''bother''' to try?}}
## To do something which is of [[negligible]] [[inconvenience]].
##: {{ux|en|You didn’t even '''bother''' to close the door.}}

====Usage notes====
* In sense 3 this is a [[catenative]] verb that takes the ''to infinitive'' or the ''gerund (-ing)''. See [[Appendix:English catenative verbs]]

#: {{syn|en|Thesaurus:commotion}}
#: {{ux|en|There was a bit of '''bother''' at the hairdresser's when they couldn't find my appointment in the book.}}
#* {{RQ:Telegraph|author=Monty Munford|title=What’s the point of carrying a mobile phone nowadays?|url=http://www.telegraph.co.uk/technology/technology-topics/11351591/Whats-the-point-of-carrying-a-mobile-phone-nowadays.html|date=18 January 2015|passage=It was a 15-minute return trip to walk back home to pick up my device, but I weighed it up and decided that it wasn’t worth the '''bother'''.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150121054616/http://www.telegraph.co.uk:80/technology/technology-topics/11351591/Whats-the-point-of-carrying-a-mobile-phone-nowadays.html|archivedate=21 January 2015}}

#: {{ux|en|Yes, I can do that for you—it’s no '''bother'''.}}

Look at your elegant clothes on the floor.” / “Oh, '''''bother'''!''” retorted Sarah.}}
